title: American Literature
description: Ten short introductions to classic American writers and their worlds: Mark Twain's river, Emily Dickinson's house, Thoreau's pond, the Alcott family, Willa Cather's plains, Steinbeck's Dust Bowl, Langston Hughes's Harlem, Harper Lee's Maycomb, a library lab and a book club.
topic: Classic American writers and their books

lessons.title: Mark Twain and the River
lessons.summary: How the Mississippi of Samuel Clemens's boyhood shaped the writer Mark Twain.
lessons.text:
Long before the world knew him as Mark Twain, Samuel Clemens was a boy in Hannibal, Missouri, a small town on the banks of the Mississippi River. He was born in 1835, and for the rest of his life the great river ran through his memory and his books.

In Hannibal, the most exciting event of the day was the arrival of a steamboat. Clemens later remembered how the whole town woke up at once. Idle men who had been sitting in front of the shops all morning jumped to their feet, and idle boys ran down to the water. Black smoke would puff from the boat's two tall chimneys, and every puff seemed to announce that the wide world had come to visit. Every boy in town, he wrote, dreamed of working on the river.

Clemens made that dream come true. In his early twenties he trained as a steamboat pilot, and in 1859 he earned his license. The job was far harder than it looked. A pilot had to know every bend, every bank of sand and every hidden tree in more than a thousand miles of river, and he had to know them at night, in fog and in rain, when visibility was close to nothing. In poor visibility, a man at the front of the boat measured the depth and called out the numbers loudly, so that the pilot could hear him over the engines. One of those calls, which meant water twelve feet deep and safe, was "mark twain." Years later, Clemens chose it as his pen name.

The Civil War closed the river to ordinary traffic in 1861, and his career as a pilot ended. He went west to Nevada and became a newspaper writer. There he earned a reputation as a joker, and the reputation was deserved. In 1864, after a quarrel with a rival editor, he came close to fighting a duel. The duel never took place: Clemens left for San Francisco instead, and later he told the story as a joke against himself.

Still, being a joker was never the whole truth about him. Much of his humor is ironic: he says one thing and quietly means the opposite. In his most famous novel, a boy named Huck Finn floats down the Mississippi on a raft and tells his own story, and through the boy's innocent voice Twain shows, with ironic force, how cruel many respectable adults can be.

In 1870 he married Olivia Langdon, the sweetheart to whom he had written long, devoted letters. For thirty-four years, until her death, she remained his sweetheart, his first reader and his most careful editor. He lived into the twentieth century and died in 1910, but in his books the river of his boyhood never stopped flowing. Twentieth-century readers found it there, wide and brown and full of life, and so do we.

Questions:
Where did Samuel Clemens grow up?
He grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, a small town on the Mississippi River.
Why did a pilot need to know the river so well?
He had to guide the boat at night and in fog, when visibility was close to nothing.
Where does the name Mark Twain come from?
It was a call, shouted loudly from the front of the boat, that meant the water was twelve feet deep and safe.
What happened after his quarrel in Nevada?
He came close to fighting a duel, but he left for San Francisco instead.

lessons.title: Emily Dickinson's Quiet House
lessons.summary: The private life of Emily Dickinson in Amherst and the unusual poems she left behind.
lessons.text:
In Amherst, Massachusetts, there is a large brick house where Emily Dickinson was born in 1830 and where she died in 1886. For most of her adult life, she rarely left it. She wore white dresses, avoided visitors and sometimes spoke to guests from behind a half-open door. People in town thought her strange, and many later readers pictured her as cold and detached from the world. The poems and letters she left behind tell a different story.

As a girl, Dickinson was lively and curious. At school she studied the science of plants, and she learned to name the reproductive parts of a flower, the parts that produce seeds. She also pressed more than four hundred plants in a large album. Her interest in the reproductive life of plants never left her: her poems are full of bees, seeds and flowers that open and close.

As she grew older, her circle grew smaller. In 1875 her mother suffered a stroke and became an invalid, unable to leave her bed. For seven years, Emily and her sister Lavinia cared for her. Looking after an invalid is slow, tiring work, and it kept Emily even closer to home. Yet a truly detached person could not have written her letters, which are warm, funny and sharp. She wrote to friends for decades, and she often sent a poem with a letter, or a flower with a poem.

Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, but only about ten were printed while she lived. She was cautious about publication, and when a few poems did appear, editors changed them without asking her. That experience may have made her more cautious still. Instead of publishing, she copied her poems by hand and sewed them into small booklets, which she kept in her room.

Her poems are short, and many readers compare them to miniature paintings: each miniature holds a whole world in a few lines. Many follow the rhythm of a hymn, the simple religious songs she heard in church every Sunday. A reader who knows a familiar hymn can often sing a Dickinson poem to the same tune. Yet the ideas inside these hymn shapes deal with death, doubt and the mind.

After her death, Lavinia found the booklets and wanted the poems published. The first editors, however, found the writing inconsistent. Dickinson used dashes everywhere and capital letters in unexpected places. The editors corrected what they saw as inconsistent habits, and it was not until 1955 that an edition faithful to her own pages appeared. Even now, scholars disagree about which version of some poems should be considered definitive, because a definitive text is hard to fix when the poet herself left several versions.

Needless to say, every reading of a Dickinson poem is somewhat subjective. Two readers may find opposite meanings in the same few lines, and both may be right. It is needless to choose between them; that subjective freedom is part of the pleasure of reading her.

Questions:
Why did people think Dickinson was detached from the world?
She rarely left her house, wore white and avoided visitors.
What did she learn when she studied plants at school?
She learned to name the reproductive parts of a flower.
Why did Emily stay even closer to home after 1875?
Her mother became an invalid, and Emily and Lavinia cared for her.
Why did the first editors change her poems?
They found her writing inconsistent, with dashes and capital letters in unexpected places.

lessons.title: Two Years at Walden Pond
lessons.summary: Why Henry David Thoreau went to live in a small cabin in the woods and what he learned there.
lessons.text:
In the summer of 1845, a young man named Henry David Thoreau moved into a small wooden cabin that he had built with his own hands. It stood in a woodland on the shore of Walden Pond, near the town of Concord, Massachusetts. Thoreau lived there for a little more than two years, and the book he wrote about the experience, Walden, became one of the most influential works in American literature.

Why would an educated man leave town to live alone in the woods? Thoreau explained that he wanted to find out how little a person really needs. Most people, he believed, worked so hard to buy things that they had no time left to live. He wanted to show that a life could be sufficiently comfortable with very few possessions, and that a person who needs little is free. His endeavor was not an escape from society but an experiment.

The cabin had one room with a bed, a table, a desk and three chairs. He cooked over a fireplace at first, and in his second winter he used a small iron stove, because the stove burned less wood. He grew beans, baked his own bread and spent less than thirty dollars on the building. He lived sufficiently well on very little, and he kept careful accounts to prove it.

Most of his days, however, were spent watching. He studied the pond in every season and compared a lake to the eye of the earth. On calm mornings its surface was serene, a smooth mirror of the sky and the trees. Even in winter, the woodland around it felt serene to him. The animals came to know him as a harmless neighbor. He never tried to tame the larger creatures, but a wild mouse that lived under his floor grew so tame that it ran over his shoes and ate from his fingers. He believed that most creatures are harmless if we leave them alone.

The peace was not complete. A railroad ran along one side of the pond, and the whistle of the train was a daily disruption. Thoreau wrote about the disruption with interest, as a sign of the busy world he had left.

During this period he also spent one night in jail. He had refused to pay a tax because he would not support a government that permitted slavery. Someone paid the tax, and he was released the next morning. He did not see himself as a martyr, and one night was too short to make him one. Yet the essay he wrote afterward, on why a person may refuse to obey a law that he believes is wrong, traveled far. In the twentieth century, leaders such as Gandhi and Martin Luther King would invoke his ideas, and peaceful protesters still invoke them today. In their hands, the man who refused to be a martyr became a teacher.

When the endeavor ended in 1847, he returned to town without regret.

Questions:
Where did Thoreau build his cabin?
He built it in a woodland on the shore of Walden Pond, near Concord.
What did Thoreau want to find out?
He wanted to find out how little a person really needs.
How did the wild mouse behave?
It grew so tame that it ran over his shoes and ate from his fingers.
What was a daily disruption at the pond?
The whistle of the train on the railroad was a daily disruption.

lessons.title: The Alcotts of Orchard House
lessons.summary: Louisa May Alcott's family, her time as a nurse and the house where she wrote Little Women.
lessons.text:
Visitors to Concord, Massachusetts, can walk into a brown wooden house where Louisa May Alcott wrote Little Women in 1868. The house, called Orchard House, has been carefully preserved, and the museum that runs it tries to recreate the rooms as the Alcott family knew them. Standing in those rooms, it is easy to see where the book's famous warmth came from.

The Alcotts were a loving family, but they were often poor. Louisa's father, Bronson Alcott, was a teacher and thinker with brilliant ideas and almost no talent for earning money. Her mother, Abigail, held the household together. There were four daughters, Anna, Louisa, Elizabeth and May, and readers of Little Women will recognize them in the four March sisters. Louisa wrote stories to support her family, and she wrote fast; one can imagine her fingers stained with ink by the end of each day, and her sleeves stained too. Her father built her a simple desk, a half-round shelf between two windows, and it can still be seen in her bedroom.

The youngest sister, May, was an artist. On the walls of her room she drew decorative figures and faces, and many of these decorative drawings survive.

Before her great success, Louisa went through a hard experience. During the Civil War, moved by a patriotic wish to serve, she volunteered as a nurse in a hospital in Washington. Many young women felt the same patriotic duty, but few understood what awaited them. Hospitals at the time had poor hygiene: doctors did not yet know how germs spread, and basic hygiene, such as washing hands and changing sheets, was often ignored. After only six weeks, Louisa caught a serious fever. Her father came to bring her home, and thankfully she survived, although her health was never quite the same again. Thankfully, too, she turned the experience into a short book about hospital life, which became her first real success.

Little Women itself began with encouragement from a publisher, who asked her to write a book for girls. Louisa was not sure she could; she said she had never liked girls much, except her own sisters. With his encouragement, she wrote about what she knew best: her own family. The book was an immediate success, and it has never been out of print.

Fame brought its own problems. Strangers arrived at the door hoping to meet the author, and Louisa disliked the fuss. It is said that she sometimes pretended to be the maid to escape the fuss of visitors.

Today, the house is full of objects the family used, and guides try to recreate the atmosphere of an ordinary evening there, with sisters reading, sewing and putting on plays for one another. The warmth of those evenings is still what readers love most in the book.

Questions:
What did May draw on the walls of her room?
She drew decorative figures and faces, and many of these drawings survive.
Why did Louisa volunteer as a nurse?
She was moved by a patriotic wish to serve during the Civil War.
Why were hospitals dangerous at the time?
They had poor hygiene, because doctors did not yet know how germs spread.
What did Louisa do when strangers came to the door?
She disliked the fuss and sometimes pretended to be the maid.

lessons.title: Willa Cather's Prairie
lessons.summary: How a childhood on the Nebraska plains gave Willa Cather the subject of her best novels.
lessons.text:
In 1883, when Willa Cather was nine years old, her family left the green hills of Virginia and moved to Nebraska. The change shocked her. Instead of forests and mountains, she saw an ocean of grass under an enormous sky. The land was thinly populated, and to a child it looked almost vacant: there were few trees, few roads and very few houses. She later remembered feeling as if the world ended at the edge of the grass.

The country was not as vacant as it seemed, however. It was being settled by families from many lands: Sweden, Norway, Germany and Bohemia, which is now part of the Czech Republic. They were unrelated people from different countries, speaking different languages, yet out on the plains they depended on one another. Unrelated families shared tools, food and news. A neighbor might arrive with a pint of milk for a sick child, and the next week receive a pint of honey in return. The young Cather rode her pony from farm to farm, listening to the immigrant women tell stories of the old country. Those stories stayed with her for the rest of her life.

Her family soon moved into the small town of Red Cloud, which was more densely populated than the farms around it. There, families with a little money rode to church on Sunday in a surrey, a light carriage with two seats and sometimes a cloth roof. A girl from a farm, walking along the road, might watch the surrey go by and wonder about a life she would never have. Cather noticed such moments, and later she put them into her novels.

She left Nebraska for college and then for a career in magazines in New York. At first she did not seem destined to write about the plains; for years her stories took place in cities. But when she finally returned to the land of her childhood, in O Pioneers! and My Ántonia, she found her true subject. Perhaps she had been destined for it all along.

Her novels show the land in all its moods. In a hard year, wind, hail and drought could ruin a family. In a good year, the bounty of the harvest filled every barn, and the wheat stood as high as a man's chest. Cather wrote about that bounty with deep feeling, but she never forgot its cost: the years of loneliness and labor that turned grass into farms.

She also loved the small details of the plains. In late summer, orange and black monarch butterflies drifted across the fields on their long journey south. A monarch can fly thousands of miles. In her books, small things like a butterfly, a wild rose or the red color of the grass in autumn receive the same care as great events.

Questions:
How did the young Cather feel when she arrived in Nebraska?
She was shocked, and the land looked almost vacant to her.
Who was settling the land around her family?
Families from Sweden, Norway, Germany and Bohemia were settling it.
How did unrelated families help one another?
They shared tools, food and news, and a neighbor might bring a pint of milk for a sick child.
What is a surrey?
It is a light carriage with two seats and sometimes a cloth roof.
What did monarch butterflies do in late summer?
They drifted across the fields on their long journey south.

lessons.title: Steinbeck and the Dust Bowl
lessons.summary: The disaster on the Great Plains and the novel John Steinbeck wrote about the families who fled it.
lessons.text:
In the early years of the Great Depression, a disaster struck the southern Great Plains of the United States. For decades, farmers had plowed up the native grass to plant wheat. Without the grass to hold it, the soil had no protection. When a long drought began, and one dry year followed another without a single rainy season, the wind began to lift the soil into the air.

The storms that followed became known as the Dust Bowl. Some were so thick that day turned to night, and people tied cloths over their faces to breathe. The worst damage was in the Texas panhandle, in the panhandle of Oklahoma, a narrow strip in the northwestern part of the state, and in nearby parts of Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico. Year after year, farmers watched the disappearance of the soil that had fed their families. Then came the disappearance of their savings, as banks took back farms whose owners could no longer pay.

Hundreds of thousands of people went west. Many of them came not from the northwestern dust region but from eastern Oklahoma and other poor farming areas, where low prices had already ruined them. They packed their furniture, children and grandparents into old cars and trucks and drove along Route 66 toward California, where they had heard there was work picking fruit. Families often traveled together in a convoy, so that one car could help another when it broke down. A convoy of overloaded trucks crawling across the desert became one of the lasting images of the time.

John Steinbeck, a young writer from California, visited the camps where these migrants lived after they arrived. The rich farms of California, with their oranges, grapes and cotton, stood beside families who were starving. There were far more workers than jobs, so wages fell, and children went hungry in the middle of plenty. He wrote newspaper articles about starving families, and then he began a novel.

The Grapes of Wrath, which appeared in 1939, follows the Joad family from Oklahoma to California. The book was a huge success, but it also made enemies. Some powerful farm owners called it leftist propaganda, and in a few places it was banned and even burned. Its defenders replied that it was not leftist propaganda but an honest picture of what Steinbeck had seen.

For the families who lived through it, the Dust Bowl was a traumatic experience, and many survivors rarely spoke about it. Such traumatic memories did not diminish easily, even after the rains returned and farmers learned new ways to protect the soil.

Today, much of the old Route 66 has been replaced by modern highways, and 18-wheelers, the huge trucks that run on eighteen wheels, roar past the small towns where migrant families once stopped. A driver in an 18-wheeler can cross Oklahoma in a few hours, a journey that took a family in a crowded car several days. The power of the book, however, does not diminish.

Questions:
Why did the wind lift the soil into the air?
The farmers had plowed up the grass, and a long drought began without a single rainy season.
Why did families travel in a convoy?
They traveled together so that one car could help another when it broke down.
What did Steinbeck find in the California camps?
He found families who were starving beside some of the richest farms in the country.
Why did some farm owners dislike the book?
They called it leftist propaganda.

lessons.title: A Haircut in Harlem
lessons.summary: A visitor gets a haircut near Langston Hughes's house and hears about the poet from the barber.
lessons.text:
On my first visit to New York, I wanted to see the neighborhood where Langston Hughes had lived, so I took the subway north to Harlem. His house is a narrow stone building on a quiet street, with steps leading up to the front door. Afterward, since my hair was far too long, I walked into a barbershop around the corner for a haircut.

The barber, an older man named Calvin, asked why I had come to Harlem. When I mentioned Hughes, he smiled and stopped cutting. "Then you've come to the right chair," he said. While he finished my haircut, he told me what he knew, and later I checked his facts in a library. He was right about almost everything.

Hughes was born in Missouri and arrived in Harlem as a young man in 1921. At that time Harlem was becoming a predominantly Black neighborhood, home to families who had moved north to escape the oppression and poverty of the South. In the following years, the neighborhood produced so much music, painting and writing that the period became known as the Harlem Renaissance, one of the great artistic movements of the twentieth century.

Hughes wrote poems that sounded like the music he heard in Harlem's clubs. He borrowed the rhythms of jazz and the blues, and he wrote about ordinary people: workers, maids, students, mothers, a man playing piano late at night. Some critics at first thought this was not serious poetry, but Hughes saw that as a misunderstanding of what poetry is for. He wanted to affirm the beauty of Black life as it really was, and he believed that to affirm a people, a writer must describe them honestly, including their struggle against oppression.

The biggest misunderstanding about Hughes, Calvin said, is that he was only a poet. He also wrote novels, plays, newspaper columns and books for children, and he was a songwriter. As a songwriter, he wrote the words for an opera that was performed on Broadway, and he worked with composers and singers throughout his life. Calvin told me that he had once heard a small jazz ensemble perform music set to Hughes's poems in a Harlem church. A small ensemble, he said, suits those poems better than a big orchestra, because every word should be heard.

While Calvin talked, a young man with a tall, round afro came in and sat down to wait. He wanted only a light trim, he said, because he was proud of his afro. He told Calvin that his grandmother used to read Hughes's poems to him, and that he still knew some by heart.

When my haircut was done, Calvin brushed off my shoulders. He said that Hughes had written about Harlem the way a son writes about his mother, with love and with honesty. Walking back to the subway, I felt that Harlem and its poet still belonged together.

Questions:
Why did the narrator go into the barbershop?
The narrator's hair was far too long, so the narrator went in for a haircut.
What kind of neighborhood was Harlem becoming in the early twentieth century?
It was becoming a predominantly Black neighborhood.
What did Hughes want his poems to affirm?
He wanted to affirm the beauty of Black life as it really was.
What did Hughes write as a songwriter?
He wrote the words for an opera that was performed on Broadway.

lessons.title: The Town of Maycomb
lessons.summary: An introduction to Harper Lee's novel about a lawyer, his children and their small Alabama town.
lessons.text:
Harper Lee grew up in Monroeville, a small town in southern Alabama, where her father was a lawyer. In 1960 she published To Kill a Mockingbird, a novel set in a town very much like her own. She called it Maycomb. The book became one of the most widely read American novels of the twentieth century, and for more than fifty years it was the only novel she published.

The story takes place during the Great Depression and is told by Scout Finch, a bold, curious girl who is six years old when it begins. Scout lives with her older brother, Jem, and their father, Atticus, a lawyer whose wife has died. In summer the children play with Dill, a boy who visits his aunt next door. Their favorite game is an imaginary drama about a man named Boo Radley, who lives on their street but never leaves his house. Nobody has seen him for years, so the children fill the empty space with imaginary stories, each more frightening than the last.

The main premise of the novel is simple and serious. Atticus is asked to defend Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of a crime against a white woman. In the Maycomb of that time, it is probable that such a man will be found guilty whatever the evidence; indeed, most of the town considers his guilt more than probable before the trial begins. Atticus agrees to defend him seriously and honestly, knowing that this will make life unpleasant for his family.

It does. Classmates insult Scout, and adults whisper about her father. Scout's first reaction to an unpleasant word is to use her fists. Atticus asks her to show restraint and to fight with her head instead. His own restraint is remarkable: when people insult him, he answers calmly, and he avoids confrontation whenever he can. Yet he does not run from every confrontation, because there are times when standing quietly in one place is the bravest thing a person can do.

Throughout the book, Atticus is a protector, not only of his client but of his children's sense of fairness. Readers have also noticed that he is a quiet protector rather than a loud hero; he never makes speeches about himself. Lee shows clearly how some citizens of Maycomb are righteous in their own eyes, sure of their goodness while they treat the Black families of the town unjustly. That righteous certainty is exactly what Atticus refuses to share.

Many readers are disturbed by what they find in the novel, and they should be. It shows a community in which injustice is ordinary. Scout herself is disturbed by much of what she sees, and through her honest eyes, readers learn to look at their own towns more carefully.

Questions:
Who tells the story of the novel?
It is told by Scout Finch, a girl who is six years old when it begins.
What is the children's favorite game?
It is an imaginary drama about a man named Boo Radley.
Why does Atticus's work make life unpleasant for his family?
He agrees to defend Tom Robinson seriously, and much of the town is against it.
What does Atticus ask Scout to do when she wants to fight?
He asks her to show restraint and to fight with her head instead.
Why are many readers disturbed by the novel?
It shows a community in which injustice is ordinary.

lessons.title: Letters in the Conservation Lab
lessons.summary: A new library worker learns how old letters by American writers are protected and photographed.
lessons.text:
Last fall I started work as an assistant in the special collections of a university library. The library owns thousands of letters written by American writers of the nineteenth century, and my job is to help keep them safe for the next two hundred years. Like every new employee, I began on probation. For six months, my supervisor, Dr. Okafor, would watch my work closely, and only at the end of the probation period would the library decide whether to keep me.

On my first morning, she explained the rules of the reading room, where scholars study the letters. Visitors may bring pencils, laptops and notebooks, but no pens. A pen cartridge can leak, and a single drop of ink from a broken cartridge can ruin a page that has survived for a century and a half.

Most of my work happens in the lab behind the reading room. Old paper is fragile: it turns yellow, grows weak and tears along its folds. Each letter we receive is cleaned with a soft brush, pressed flat and placed in a clear sleeve made of a stable polymer, a kind of plastic that does not release harmful chemicals as it ages. The polymer lets a reader see both sides of the page without touching it. The sleeves then go into special boxes, and each box is divided into compartments, one compartment for each group of letters, so that nothing slides or bends.

Every time someone handles a letter, it suffers a small disturbance, so we try to make each disturbance count. That is why the library is photographing its whole collection. The photography apparatus fills a corner of the lab: a large camera on a steel frame above a soft, padded stand. The letter stays stationary on the stand while the camera moves above it, because moving the paper would be riskier than moving the apparatus. Once a letter has been photographed, scholars around the world can study it on a screen, and the original can rest in its box.

At first I worked slowly, terrified of making a mistake. Dr. Okafor told me that working efficiently is not the same as working fast. To work efficiently, she said, you plan each movement before your hands touch the paper.

We also prepare for disasters. The library stands near a river, so it has a written evacuation plan for floods. Every box carries a number that shows its priority, and twice a year we practice an evacuation, carrying the most valuable boxes up to the top floor and keeping each one level and stationary in our arms.

In March, my probation ended, and I was offered a permanent position. On the same day, I was trusted for the first time to clean a letter written by a famous poet in a small, careful hand.

Questions:
What happened during the narrator's probation?
The narrator's supervisor watched the narrator's work closely for six months.
Why are pens not allowed in the reading room?
A pen cartridge can leak, and a drop of ink can ruin an old page.
What does the polymer sleeve do?
It protects the letter and lets a reader see both sides without touching it.
Why does the letter stay stationary during photography?
Moving the paper would be riskier than moving the apparatus.
What does the library practice twice a year?
It practices an evacuation, carrying the most valuable boxes up to the top floor.

lessons.title: A Book Club Across the World
lessons.summary: A retired librarian's book club for classic American novels meets over pancakes and online.
lessons.text:
When Helen retired after thirty years as a school librarian, she missed talking about books. So she started a book club for classic American novels. Once a month, the members meet for breakfast at a small restaurant on Main Street. The building has a colorful history: in the seventies it was a disco, and the owner still keeps the old disco ball hanging above the counter, although it has not turned in decades. The restaurant is famous for its pancakes, and the members joke that they choose long novels so that the talk lasts as long as a stack of pancakes. The owner makes her own blueberry syrup, and Helen always asks for extra syrup.

Not every member can come to the restaurant, so the club also meets online. Helen's niece, Grace, lives in Australia and joins the discussion by video. Because of the time difference, it is late evening there, and once a kangaroo hopped across the lawn outside the window behind her while she was talking about Huckleberry Finn. Since then, the members ask about the kangaroo at every meeting.

To help members find one another online, Grace created a hashtag for the club. Every time someone posts a photo of a book or a favorite line, they add the hashtag, and Helen's phone makes a small ding. On some days the ding sounds every few minutes, and Helen has learned to turn the sound off during dinner.

Helen reads on a lightweight electronic reader, because her eyes are not what they used to be and she can make the letters as large as she likes. The device is so lightweight that she can hold it in one hand for hours. When the screen suddenly stopped working last spring, she was relieved to find that it was still under warranty. The store replaced it for free, and since then she reads the warranty of everything she buys.

One member, a college student named Leo, writes reviews for a small literary magazine online. He always calls it "the mag," as if it were a friend. Last month the mag published his review of a Willa Cather novel, and he read it aloud to the club between pancakes.

When the club's page became popular, an advertiser offered to pay for space on it. Helen thought about the offer for a week and then said no. She did not want an advertiser to have any influence on what the club read or said. The members agreed, and the owner of the restaurant, who had heard the story, gave everyone a free cup of coffee at the next meeting.

At their last meeting, they finished The Grapes of Wrath. Grace said that it felt strange to read about the Dust Bowl during a dry Australian summer. Helen answered that this was exactly what good books do: they travel.

Questions:
Where does the book club meet once a month?
It meets for breakfast at a small restaurant that was once a disco.
How does Grace join the discussion?
She joins by video from Australia, and once a kangaroo hopped across the lawn behind her.
What happens when someone uses the club's hashtag?
Helen's phone makes a small ding.
Why was Helen relieved when her reader stopped working?
It was still under warranty, so the store replaced it for free.
Why did Helen say no to the advertiser?
She did not want an advertiser to have any influence on what the club read or said.
